newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI April 15 report seen stern but uncontroversial.
newsitem.headline: EMI April 15 report seen stern but uncontroversial.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) is gearing up to reveal what it thinks about the development of Europe's euro single currency but its annual report next week is unlikely to break controversial ground, economists say.

While the precurcor organistion of a European Central Bank (ECB) is likely to take a tough line on the persistent lack of convergence on public finances among EU states, the overall tone of its comments is likely to be studiously bland.
"The EMI will steer away from all the hot potatoes," said Thomas Mayer, senior economists at Goldman Sachs, Germany.
"This will be a simple recap of events in the past and will attempt to be as objective as possible," he said.

The EMI's comments will be released in its third annual report, due for release on Tuesday April 15 at 1500 GMT to coincide with a news conference with Alexandre Lamfalussy, the institute's outgoing president.

The report will mainly list historical information on developments of the past year but should also contain a certain amount of comment on efforts by EU states to make the grade for the planned single currency launch on January 1 1999.

In its last report, the EMI clearly pinpointed lack of convergence on public finances as the biggest obstacle for the euro project, and said sluggish economic conditions were no excuse for countries to lag in this regard.

The Maastricht Treaty calls for national debts to total no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- or at least to show significant progress in falling toward this level -- and for budget deficits to be three percent or less except in exceptional circumstances.

Prospects for an on-the-button fulfilment of these demands have become increasingly dim since last year, with economists widely predicting that Germany, the linchpin of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) project, will overshoot the three percent deficit reference level by far.
The EMI is likely to sternly re-emphasise the importance of sustainable fulfilment of EMU budgetary goals.
"The tone could be sharpened in terms of public convergence," said Mayer. "After all, time is passing and the process of convergence leaves a lot to be desired."

But since the contents of the report will have been approved by all 15 members of the EMI council, each the head of an EU central bank, the chances that it will contain any politically charged comments are extremely slim.
"The past reports have been backward-looking," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
"This will be an update on the data. It won't contain anything that will exclude a political decision (on which member states are likely to qualify "

Economists will, however, be looking for more hints as to the make-up of the European Central Bank's monetary policy toolkit, after the EMI's January framework report on the ECB left several key issues unresolved.
But there will be no definitive resolution of these issues until the ECB takes over power from the EMI next year.

The main outstanding issues are whether the ECB will guide monetary policy by watching money supply developments or by directly observing inflation, and whether the new bank will levy the highly unpopular non-interest bearing minimum reserve requirements from banks which are favoured by the Bundesbank.

The report may also include a reassuring message on the vexed question of how much clout the European Central Bank will carry, or whether politicians would try to gain influence over it via a planned stability council of finance ministers.

Despite repeated assurances from politicians that the ECB's independence is guaranteed, largely supported by Lamfalussy himself, markets have been concerned that politicians will exert far more influence over the euro central bank than Bonn, for instance, exerts on the mighty Bundesbank.
